notes:
Basics

  • Set: well-defined collection. Roster form $\{1,2,3\}$; set-builder $\{x : x \in \mathbb N, x < 4\}$.
  • Empty set $\phi$; singleton; finite/infinite; equal sets; subset $A \subseteq B$; proper subset $A \subset B$.
  • Set with $n$ elements has $2^n$ subsets, $2^n - 1$ proper subsets, and $|P(A)| = 2^n$. $P(\phi) = \{\phi\}$ has 1 element.
  • Intervals: $(a,b)$ open, $[a,b]$ closed, $(a,b]$, $[a,b)$.

Operations

  • $A \cup B$, $A \cap B$, $A - B = \{x : x\in A, x\notin B\}$, complement $A' = U - A$, symmetric difference $A\,\Delta\,B = (A-B)\cup(B-A)$.
  • If $A \subseteq B$: $A \cup B = B$, $A \cap B = A$.
  • De Morgan: $(A\cup B)' = A'\cap B'$, $(A\cap B)' = A'\cup B'$.
  • $A - B = A \cap B'$; $A \cap A' = \phi$; $A \cup A' = U$.

Counting

  • $n(A\cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A\cap B)$.
  • $n(A\cup B\cup C) = n(A)+n(B)+n(C) - n(A\cap B) - n(B\cap C) - n(A\cap C) + n(A\cap B\cap C)$.
  • Neither $= n(U) - n(A\cup B)$. Only $A = n(A) - n(A\cap B)$.
  • $n(A\times B) = n(A)\,n(B)$; number of relations from $A$ to $B$ $= 2^{n(A)n(B)}$.

Exam tip

Usually 1 question, almost always on counting (union/intersection word problem) or number of subsets. Quick marks — never lose them.

questions.q: If $n(A) = 20$, $n(B) = 30$ and $n(A\cap B) = 10$, then $n(A\cup B)$ is
questions.trick: Union formula: add both, then subtract the overlap once.

questions.q: The number of proper subsets of a set containing 5 elements is
questions.explanation: $2^5 - 1 = 31$ (the set itself is excluded).
questions.trick: Proper subsets $= 2^n - 1$; exclude the set itself.

questions.q: The number of elements in the power set of the empty set is
questions.explanation: $P(\phi) = \{\phi\}$, which has one element.
questions.trick: $P(\phi) = \{\phi\}$ always has exactly 1 element.

questions.q: If $A \subset B$, then $A \cap B$ and $A \cup B$ are respectively
questions.explanation: Every element of $A$ is in $B$, so the intersection is $A$ and the union is $B$.
questions.trick: $A\subset B$: intersection is smaller set $A$, union is bigger set $B$.

questions.q: $(A \cup B)'$ is equal to
questions.explanation: De Morgan's law.
questions.trick: De Morgan: complement of union = intersection of complements.

questions.q: In a class of 60 students, 25 play cricket, 20 play football and 10 play both. The number of students who play neither game is
questions.trick: Neither $=$ total $- n(A\cup B)$.

questions.q: If $n(A) = 3$ and $n(B) = 4$, the number of relations from $A$ to $B$ is
questions.explanation: A relation is a subset of $A\times B$, which has 12 elements; number of subsets $= 2^{12}$.
questions.trick: Relations from $A$ to $B$ $= 2^{n(A)n(B)}$, not $n(A)n(B)$ itself.

questions.q: The set $\{x : x \in \mathbb R, -2 < x \le 5\}$ in interval notation is
questions.explanation: $-2$ is excluded (round bracket), 5 is included (square bracket).
questions.trick: Round bracket = point excluded, square bracket = point included.

questions.q: Which of the following is an empty set?
options: $\{x : x \text{ is an even prime greater than 2}\}$
questions.explanation: 2 is the only even prime, so there is no even prime greater than 2. The others give $\{2\}$, $\{2\}$ and $\{0\}$.
questions.trick: 2 is the only even prime — check that edge case first.

questions.explanation: $A - B = \{1,2\}$, $B - A = \{5,6\}$; union $= \{1,2,5,6\}$ (the symmetric difference).
questions.trick: $(A-B)\cup(B-A)$ = elements belonging to exactly one set.

questions.q: If a set $A$ has 64 subsets, then $n(A)$ is
questions.explanation: $2^n = 64 \Rightarrow n = 6$.
questions.trick: Solve $2^n =$ given subset count for $n$.

questions.explanation: $x^2 - 5x + 6 = (x-2)(x-3) = 0 \Rightarrow A = \{2, 3\}$, a proper subset of $B$.
questions.trick: Factor the equation into a set first, then compare with $B$.

questions.q: In a survey of 100 people, 60 like tea, 50 like coffee and 30 like both. The number of people who like exactly one of the two is
questions.explanation: Only tea $= 60 - 30 = 30$; only coffee $= 50 - 30 = 20$; exactly one $= 50$.
questions.trick: Exactly one $=$ (only $A$) $+$ (only $B$), not the plain union.

questions.q: $A \cap (B \cup C)$ is equal to
questions.explanation: Distributive law of intersection over union.
questions.trick: $\cap$ distributes over $\cup$: $A\cap(B\cup C)=(A\cap B)\cup(A\cap C)$.

questions.explanation: $A\cup B\cup C = \{1,2,3,4,5\}$, which has 5 elements.
questions.trick: List all distinct elements once; that count is $n(A\cup B\cup C)$.

questions.q: The symmetric difference $A \triangle B$ is defined as
questions.explanation: $A\triangle B = (A-B)\cup(B-A)$, which equals $(A\cup B) - (A\cap B)$.
questions.trick: Symmetric difference = union minus intersection.

questions.q: If a set has 4 elements, the number of subsets containing a particular fixed element of the set is
questions.explanation: Fix that element; the remaining 3 elements can each be included or not, giving $2^3 = 8$ such subsets.
questions.trick: Fix one element; remaining $n-1$ are free $\Rightarrow 2^{n-1}$ subsets.

questions.q: $A - B$ is equal to
questions.explanation: $A - B$ consists of elements of $A$ that are not in $B$, i.e. $A \cap B'$.
questions.trick: $A-B$ always equals $A\cap B'$.

questions.q: Which of the following sets is infinite?
questions.explanation: $\{x : x\in\mathbb N\}$ is the set of all natural numbers, which is infinite; the other three are finite.
questions.trick: $\mathbb N$ itself is infinite; equation-defined sets are usually finite.

questions.q: If $A = \{1,2,3\}$ and $B = \{p,q,r\}$, then $A$ and $B$ are
questions.explanation: $A$ and $B$ have the same number of elements (3) but different elements, so they are equivalent but not equal.
questions.trick: Same element count but different elements $=$ equivalent, not equal.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is FALSE?
questions.explanation: $A \cap A' = \phi$, not $U$; the other three statements are standard set identities.
questions.trick: $A\cap A'$ is always $\phi$, never $U$ — spot the fake identity.

questions.q: If $A$ and $B$ are disjoint sets, then $n(A\cup B)$ equals
questions.explanation: For disjoint sets $n(A\cap B) = 0$, so $n(A\cup B) = n(A) + n(B)$.
questions.trick: Disjoint $\Rightarrow n(A\cap B)=0$, so union is just the sum.

questions.q: In a survey of 100 students, 40 study Physics, 30 study Chemistry, 30 study Mathematics, 10 study both Physics and Chemistry, 8 study both Chemistry and Mathematics, 6 study both Physics and Mathematics, and 5 study all three subjects. How many students study none of the three subjects?
questions.explanation: $n(P\cup C\cup M) = 40+30+30-10-8-6+5 = 81$. Students studying none $= 100 - 81 = 19$.
questions.trick: Inclusion-exclusion: $+$singles $-$pairs$+$triple, then subtract from total.

questions.q: If $n(P(A)) = 256$, then $n(A)$ is
questions.explanation: $2^n = 256 = 2^8 \Rightarrow n = 8$.
questions.trick: Solve $2^n = $ given power-set size directly for $n$.

questions.q: Which pair of sets is disjoint?
questions.explanation: $\{2,4,6\}$ (even numbers) and $\{1,3,5\}$ (odd numbers) share no common element; the other pairs all overlap.
questions.trick: Evens and odds share nothing — the classic disjoint pair.

questions.q: If $A \subseteq B$ and $B \subseteq A$, then
questions.explanation: Mutual containment of two sets means they have exactly the same elements, so $A = B$.
questions.trick: Mutual containment $A\subseteq B$ and $B\subseteq A$ forces $A=B$.

questions.q: If $\{a, 1, 3\} = \{2, 1, 3\}$ (as sets), then $a$ equals
questions.explanation: For the two sets to be equal, every element must match, so $a = 2$.
questions.trick: Match up the one unmatched element between the two set listings.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the null set $\phi$ is INCORRECT?
options: $\phi$ is a subset of every set
$\phi$ has exactly one subset, namely itself
questions.explanation: $\{0\}$ is a set containing the element $0$, so it has one element, while $\phi$ has none; hence $\phi \ne \{0\}$.
questions.trick: $\phi$ has zero elements; $\{0\}$ has one — never equate them.

questions.q: If $n(A) = n(B) = 17$ and $n(A\cup B) = 30$, then $n(A\cap B)$ is
questions.trick: $n(A\cap B) = n(A)+n(B)-n(A\cup B)$.

questions.explanation: $A'$ contains the elements of $U$ not in $A$, i.e. $\{6,7,8,9,10\}$.
questions.trick: Complement $=$ universal set minus $A$.

questions.q: In a Venn diagram of three sets $A$, $B$, $C$, the region representing elements in both $A$ and $B$ but not in $C$ is given by
questions.explanation: Elements in $A\cap B$ but excluding $C$ form $(A\cap B)\cap C'$.
questions.trick: In $A$ and $B$ but not $C$: write $(A\cap B)\cap C'$.

questions.q: If $n(A) = 5$ and $n(B) = 8$, the maximum possible value of $n(A\cup B)$ is
questions.explanation: The union is largest when $A$ and $B$ are disjoint: $n(A\cup B) = 5 + 8 = 13$.
questions.trick: Union is largest when the sets are disjoint — just add.

questions.q: If $n(A) = 5$ and $n(B) = 8$, the minimum possible value of $n(A\cup B)$ is
questions.explanation: The union is smallest when $A \subseteq B$, giving $n(A\cup B) = n(B) = 8$.
questions.trick: Union is smallest when the smaller set sits inside the bigger one.

questions.q: The set $\{x : x \text{ is a distinct letter in the word 'ALLOWED'}\}$ has how many elements?
questions.explanation: The distinct letters are A, L, O, W, E, D — 6 elements (the repeated L is counted once).
questions.trick: Count each repeated letter only once.

questions.q: If a set $A$ has 3 elements, the number of subsets of $A$ that contain exactly 2 elements is
questions.explanation: The number of 2-element subsets of a 3-element set is $^3C_2 = 3$.
questions.trick: Choosing $r$ elements from $n$: use $^nC_r$, not a power of 2.

questions.q: Consider the statements: (I) Every subset of a finite set is finite. (II) The empty set is a subset of every set. Which of these is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Both statements are standard facts about finite sets and the null set.
questions.trick: The empty set is a subset of every set — always true.

questions.q: If $A = \{1,2,3,4,5\}$ and $B = \{4,5,6,7\}$, then $n(A \triangle B)$ is
questions.explanation: $A - B = \{1,2,3\}$ and $B - A = \{6,7\}$, so $A\triangle B = \{1,2,3,6,7\}$, which has 5 elements.
questions.trick: Symmetric difference count: add elements unique to each set.

questions.q: If a set $A$ has $n$ elements, the number of subsets of $A$ that do NOT contain a particular fixed element is
questions.explanation: Excluding the fixed element, each of the remaining $n-1$ elements can be included or not, giving $2^{n-1}$ subsets.
questions.trick: Excluding one fixed element still leaves $2^{n-1}$ subsets.

questions.q: For two sets $A$ and $B$ with $n(A) = p$ and $n(B) = q$ where $p < q$, which of the following is always true?
questions.explanation: Since $A\cap B \subseteq A$, $n(A\cap B) \le n(A) = p$; since $B \subseteq A\cup B$, $n(A\cup B) \ge n(B) = q$. These hold regardless of how $A$ and $B$ overlap.
questions.trick: $A\cap B\subseteq$ smaller set; $A\cup B\supseteq$ bigger set, always.

questions.q: In a survey, 30 people like tea only, 20 like coffee only, and 15 like both tea and coffee. If everyone surveyed likes at least one of the two drinks, the total number of people surveyed is
questions.explanation: Total $= 30 (\text{tea only}) + 20 (\text{coffee only}) + 15 (\text{both}) = 65$.
questions.trick: Total $=$ only-$A$ $+$ only-$B$ $+$ both, no double counting needed.
